title: Why Wi-Fi Signals Pass Through Glass But Die in Walls — Engineering Cheat Sheet
subtitle: Physics-based propagation logic for network performance and signal optimization.
summary: Wi-Fi signals operate as electromagnetic waves that experience varying degrees of attenuation based on material permittivity and conductivity. Understanding these interactions is critical for engineers designing stable IoT deployments, high-density office networks, or reliable edge computing connectivity.

key_concepts.name: Electromagnetic Attenuation
key_concepts.detail: Signal loss occurs when energy is converted to heat via absorption or reflected by high-density materials like concrete, brick, or metal, which possess high dielectric constants.

key_concepts.name: Material Permittivity
key_concepts.detail: Glass has low permittivity, allowing waves to pass with minimal phase shift. Walls, particularly reinforced concrete, contain rebar acting as a Faraday cage, reflecting or trapping signals.

key_concepts.name: Fresnel Zone Clearance
key_concepts.detail: Beyond simple Line-of-Sight, RF performance requires clearance of the Fresnel zone to avoid phase cancellation caused by reflections off nearby physical obstacles and surfaces.

code_cheatsheet.explanation: Quickly assess signal strength (dBm) and link quality to identify environmental interference or material blocking.
Calculates Free Space Path Loss (FSPL) in dB; baseline metric before accounting for wall/obstacle penetration loss (dB attenuation factor).

best_practices: Prioritize line-of-sight placement for Access Points to avoid multi-wall penetration.
Use 2.4GHz for better penetration through physical obstacles compared to the shorter-range 5GHz/6GHz bands.
Perform a site survey using heatmap software to identify signal shadow zones caused by high-density materials.
Deploy mesh nodes or wired backhaul APs when physical barriers introduce >20dB of signal attenuation.

interview_qa.question: Why does a 5GHz signal drop off significantly faster than 2.4GHz when passing through a brick wall?
interview_qa.answer: Higher frequency signals have shorter wavelengths, which are more easily absorbed by the molecules in dense materials like brick. Furthermore, high-frequency signals exhibit lower diffraction capabilities, making it harder for them to 'bend' around obstacles compared to the longer wavelengths of 2.4GHz.
